extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and students of astronomy / history of science
extracted.subtask_description: A popular-science essay/chapter evaluating the Nebular Hypothesis: it critiques the idea that nebulae are remote 'island universes' and outlines a condensation/aggregation mechanism (flocculi, rotation, spiral formation) that accounts for observed nebular and solar-system phenomena. Aimed at informed lay readers and students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telescopic resolving power vs. claimed nebula distances
rubrics_metrics.description: The same instrument which decomposes hosts of nebulae into stars fails to resolve completely our own Milky Way; an instrument that shows distant clusters as separate specks could not separate remote clusters into stars if those clusters were as remote as supposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses a homely analogy (man among a swarm of bees) and numeric scaling (distances: Earth–Sun, Sirius, nebulae) to show the absurd implication that a star rendered invisible by distance would become visible if taken far further off. Antipattern: accepting the remote-galaxy interpretation despite contradictions in what a given telescope can resolve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not infer distances from apparent magnitude/size alone
rubrics_metrics.description: The tacit assumption that differences of apparent magnitude among the stars result mainly from differences of distance is 'purely gratuitous' and now proves inadmissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 61 Cygni (almost invisible) has a greater parallax than a Cygni, showing 'telescopic stars' can be nearer than Sirius; therefore relative visibilities do not reliably indicate relative distances. Evaluations should not base distance inferences solely on apparent size or brightness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolvability must be consistent with nebula size/distance
rubrics_metrics.description: If larger nebulae were nearer and smaller ones further, the largest should be the most easily resolved; but the fact is the largest nebulae are often wholly irresolvable while many quite small nebulae are easily resolved by far less powerful telescopes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete counterexample: an instrument that shows Andromeda (2.5° × 1°) as diffuse light decomposes a 15' nebula into 20,000 starry points. A plausible theory must explain this reverse pattern of resolvability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magellanic clouds: coexistence of resolvable stars and irresolvable nebulosity
rubrics_metrics.description: Within objects like the Magellanic clouds, one finds 'upwards of six hundred stars of the seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth magnitudes, nearly three hundred nebulæ, and ... irresolvable nebulosity' coexisting within small relative distance differences; this contradicts the remote-galaxy interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted authorities (Sir John Herschel, Arago) show that either one must accept impossibly enormous single stars or invisible huge star-clusters; thus the conclusion is the nebulae are not extremely remote galaxies but members of our sidereal system. A valid account must reconcile such coexistence without invoking absurd stellar sizes or invisibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irregular, indefinite outlines and irresolvability indicate early condensation stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Large, diffuse nebulae that are irregular in form and have indefinite outlines (fading insensibly into darkness) are characteristic of masses not yet gathered by mutual attraction; their largeness, irregularity, and irresolvability are significant in indicating an early stage of condensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References Arago's comparison of nebula outlines to cloud figures tossed by winds. A successful explanatory model should predict that widely-diffused, irregular nebulae will be largely irresolvable and have fading outlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spiral nebulae morphology explained by rotating medium and flocculi dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: The curves of luminous matter in spiral nebulae are those one would expect from masses whose movements are modified by rotation of the medium; spiral streaks converging to a luminous, more-resolvable centre arise naturally from flocculi drawn into a rotating medium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theory should account for spirals (not produced by discrete masses simply starting from rest) and for a central mass that is more luminous and more resolvable due to aggregation and coalescence of flocculi.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanics of flocculi aggregation: formation of rotation and vortical groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Precipitated molecules aggregate into flocculi; asymmetrical shapes and movement through a resisting medium cause deflections and divergences that, via mutual interactions and imparted motion to the medium, produce rotation of the whole mass and spiraling convergence of flocculi toward the common centre of gravity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details: collisions, dissipation, resisting medium density gradient, deflection by non-symmetric faces, and imparting motion to the medium lead to rotation; local aggregation then forms vortical groups and rotating spheroids. A valid mechanism must include these factors to explain observed motions and structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject assumption of uniform angular velocity across a nebula
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticisms (e.g., Babinet, Prof. Newcomb) assuming equal angular velocities for all parts of a nebulous spheroid are inadmissible; the condensation process implies outer portions acquire greater angular velocities than inner parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model evaluations should avoid assuming uniform angular velocity; instead allow differential angular velocities (outer parts possibly faster) which change contraction dynamics and explain observed features such as equatorial belts and ring formation without requiring equal angular speeds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cometary orbits and directions as evidence of nebular origin
rubrics_metrics.description: Fragments left behind by a condensing nebula will have extremely eccentric or non-elliptic paths, will come from all parts of the heavens, and will travel both direct and retrograde — matching the observed variety and roughly equal numbers of direct and retrograde comet orbits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observational data: of 262 recorded comets since 1680, 130 are direct and 132 retrograde; comets' orbits often classed parabolic but may be highly eccentric ellipses. A satisfactory theory must predict these orbital characteristics and the isotropic directions of arrival.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical constitution of comets explained by insufficient mass for condensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Detached fragments of nebulous matter of small mass cannot generate sufficient mutual gravitation to overcome interatomic repulsion and so will remain in a nebulous state; this accounts for cometary constitution (swarms of meteors/enveloping aeriform matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes likely origins of periodic vs non-periodic comets; small fragments remain diffuse, so comet composition and behavior should be predicted by the mass-dependent condensation mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solar System harmonies as constraints on origin theories (Laplace's evidences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Leading evidences for a common genetic process: 1) planets move in same direction and nearly same plane; 2) satellites move in same direction as planets; 3) rotations of bodies and Sun are largely in same direction as orbital motions and in similar planes; 4) small eccentricities of planets/satellites vs large eccentricities of cometary orbits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any theory of origin must explain these harmonies quantitatively; Laplace calculated the probability of such concordance arising by chance as extraordinarily small. Use these four tests as key criteria when evaluating models of Solar System formation.
